JSON: Name: moma_ac_pipeline Title: A preference-conditioned centralised actor–critic framework for learning Pareto-efficient policies in continuous multi-objective multi-agent reinforcement learning Short Hypothesis: Conditioning a centralised vector-valued critic and a shared, preference-conditioned multi-headed actor under a CTDE training regime yields higher expected utility and larger Pareto hypervolume than (a) independent per-agent preference-conditioned training and (b) outer-loop scalarisation baselines in continuous multi-objective multi-agent control tasks. Related Work: Existing work splits into three strands: single-agent multi-objective RL (MORL) methods that either run multiple single-objective trainings per preference (outer-loop scalarisation) or condition a single policy on preferences (inner-loop), single-objective multi-agent RL (MARL) actor–critic CTDE methods that stabilise multi-agent training via centralised critics but assume scalar rewards, and a small set of MOMARL approaches that either (i) collapse vector rewards to fixed scalars and apply MARL, (ii) operate only in discrete action/state spaces, or (iii) use outer-loop multi-policy solutions requiring a separate training run per preference. Limitations across these approaches include sample inefficiency of outer-loop re-training, instability and non-stationarity when agents train fully decentralised, lack of mechanisms to represent a family of Pareto-optimal policies in continuous-action multi-agent domains, and algorithmic brittleness from single-critic value estimation leading to optimistic bias. Methods that address credit assignment in MARL do not natively support vector-valued returns or preference-conditioned policy families in continuous control. Abstract: We address continuous multi-objective multi-agent reinforcement learning where cooperating agents must learn coordinated policies that trade off conflicting objectives. We propose a training framework that conditions a shared, multi-headed actor and a centralised vector-valued critic on user preference weights and follows centralised training with decentralised execution. The approach compresses a family of Pareto-aligned policies into a single conditional actor while using joint-state critics to provide stable coordination signals across agents. The main contribution is an inner-loop actor–critic pipeline for continuous multi-agent multi-objective control that produces a diverse, high-quality coverage set of trade-off policies in one training run. Expected outcomes include improved expected utility and hypervolume over independent per-agent preference training and outer-loop scalarisation baselines, stable scalability with increasing agent count, and a demonstrable reduction in optimistic utility estimation when using dual critic estimators. The framework aims to serve as a practical baseline for preference-aware continuous multi-agent systems. Experiments: Datasets/environments: Integrated continuous-control MOMARL benchmark constructed by combining multi-agent MuJoCo decompositions with vector-valued reward variants (equivalently: MaMuJoCo + multi-objective reward suite). Tasks and decompositions: Hopper (1, 3 agents), HalfCheetah (1, 2, 6 agents), Walker (1, 2 agents). Training budget: 500,000 timesteps per run, 10 random seeds per configuration. Preference sampling: Uniform draws from the simplex per episode; evaluation grid uses 100 equally spaced weights. Evaluation protocol: At each evaluation point (every 100 episodes and final), for each of 100 weights run 5 deterministic episodes and average returns; compute approximate coverage set from non-dominated mean vectors. Baselines: (1) Independent per-agent preference-conditioned MO-TD3 (each agent trains its own conditional policy without centralised critic), (2) Outer-loop multi-agent TD3 (train separate MA-TD3 policies on a fixed grid of preferences), (3) Single-critic variant of the proposed framework. Primary metrics: Expected Utility Metric (EUM) averaged over n=50 sampled preferences; Hypervolume (HV) with reference point (-1000,-1000); Cardinality of non-dominated set; Sparsity of Pareto front. Additional metric: utility estimation error (predicted scalarised critic value vs realised remaining return) computed by sampling random timesteps and preferences. Statistical testing: two-sided Welch's t-test for pairwise comparisons (alpha=0.05). Ablation studies: (A) dual-critic vs single-critic (measure estimation bias and final EUM/HV), (B) shared-trunk multi-headed actor vs independently parameterised per-agent actors (measure sample efficiency and final metrics), (C) preference sampling frequency (per-episode vs per-timestep), (D) backbone algorithm effects (TD3-style components: clipped target noise, delayed updates vs DDPG-style single-critic). Scalability study: evaluate metric changes when increasing agent count per morphology. Reporting: mean and standard deviation across seeds, learning curves, final metrics, and significance tests. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Overestimation / optimistic bias: single-critic centralised estimators may produce optimistic scalarised utilities, degrading policy selection and Pareto quality; dual-critic reduction may only partially mitigate. 2) Non-stationarity and partial observability: centralised critics require joint observations at training time but decentralised execution may still suffer credit-assignment issues in complex decompositions. 3) Sample inefficiency: conditioning a single actor on preferences increases task complexity and may need large sample budgets to approximate full Pareto coverage, especially for high-dimensional agents. 4) Scalability and compute: joint-state critics scale with agent and observation dimensionality; memory and compute cost may limit applicability to many-agent or high-degree decompositions. 5) Preference-space coverage: uniform sampling on the simplex and linear scalarisation can miss non-convex front regions and produce uneven coverage; results depend on sampling design and scalarisation choice. 6) Evaluation bias: hypervolume and reference-point choices influence comparisons; limited objectives (two-objective focus) may not generalise to many-objective settings. 7) Simulator generality: MuJoCo-based benchmarks may not reflect all real-world dynamics or competitive/mixed-motive interactions, limiting external validity. 8) Sensitivity to hyperparameters: backbone algorithm components (noise clipping, target smoothing, update frequencies) can materially affect outcomes and require problem-specific tuning.
